Until May 2000, the US made public GPS wrong on purpose, by about a street. 🛰️

It was called Selective Availability. When President Clinton switched it off, ordinary receivers got roughly 10× more accurate overnight.

And your phone still never talks to the satellites. About 30 of them broadcast where they are and exactly when each signal left. Your phone times the signals, turns them into distances, and finds the one spot where they all agree. A fourth satellite fixes your phone's clock.

Would you have guessed GPS used to be blurred on purpose? 👇

#gps #history #techexplained #howitworks #space

Before a card machine can take your money, it has to power your card. ⚡

Your bank card has no battery. The reader makes a magnetic field that cycles 13.56 million times a second, and a coil hidden around the card's edge turns it into just enough electricity to wake the chip. The chip answers with your card number plus a one-time code that only works for that payment.

On the London Tube, the gate checks the card is genuine on the spot and the bank settles up later, so nobody waits.

Did you know your card was just plastic until you tap? 👇

#contactless #nfc #howitworks #techexplained #engineering

How do you fake a traffic jam? 99 phones and a little red wagon. 🛒📱

In 2020, artist Simon Weckert pulled 99 phones running Google Maps down empty Berlin streets. Maps painted those streets red.

It worked because Maps doesn't watch roads. Phones navigating with it share their location and speed, and when lots of them crawl along one road, that stretch turns red. Maps blends that with the usual traffic for that hour to pick your route.

What other app do you think runs on data from your phone? 👇

#googlemaps #techexplained #howitworks #engineering #traffic

Your app outgrew one database server. Copies won't save you, because every write still lands on one machine.

So you split the users. A shard key like userId % 4 sends user 42 straight to shard 2, and each server only carries its slice of the reads and writes.

The catch: questions about all users hit every shard, a bad key creates a hot shard, and adding shards means moving data. That's why most apps try caching and replicas first.

Would you shard by user ID or by region? 👇

#databases #systemdesign #backend #softwareengineering #coding

How a QR code works: your phone spots the three corner squares, straightens the grid and reads each square, with backup data that rebuilds a smudged code. Denso's team gave those corners a stripe pattern that's rare in print.

#qrcode #howitworks #techexplained #engineering #smartphone

You booked a flight and a hotel. The flight went through. The hotel failed 😬

Think of a vault with two keys 🔐 It only opens when both keys turn.

Two-phase commit works the same way: a coordinator asks every service "can you?" All yes, everyone commits. One no, everyone cancels.

That's Google Spanner, and it's built into PostgreSQL.

Ever been charged for half a booking? 👇

#systemdesign #softwareengineering #backend #distributedsystems #databases

Database partitioning explained: split a billion-row table into monthly partitions by date, inside the same database. Queries for last week skip the old months, and old data drops in one step.
What's the biggest table in your app? 🗂️

#partitioning #database #postgresql #systemdesign #sql

Database replication explained: a leader sends every change to live copies in other racks, data centers or cities, so failover can promote a copy when it dies. Sync is safer, async is faster but can lose the newest writes, and replication is not a backup.
Do your copies wait to confirm, or say done right away? 🗄️

#replication #databasereplication #systemdesign #distributedsystems #backend

How Face ID works in the dark: an infrared flood light and 30,000+ invisible dots let your iPhone build a 3D depth map of your face, so a flat photo can't unlock it. In 2017 a Vietnamese security firm claimed a $150 3D mask fooled it, but key test details were missing.

3D head: "Infinite, 3D Head Scan" by Lee Perry-Smith (Infinite-Realities), CC BY 3.0.

#faceid #iphone #howitworks #techexplained #cybersecurity

Jet engine turbine blades spin in gas hotter than their own melting point. Single-crystal metal, cooling holes and a ceramic coat keep them alive 🔥

#jetengine #aerospace #turbine #materialsscience #aviation

Database sharding explained: split your users across several database servers with a shard key like userId % 4. Faster reads and writes, but cross-shard queries, hot shards and resharding are the cost.
At what size would you shard your database? 🧩

#sharding #databasesharding #systemdesign #distributedsystems #backend

Kingda Ka hit 128 mph in 3.5 seconds. Stopping it took magnets, copper and zero contact 🧲

#engineering #physics #rollercoaster #magnetism #howitsengineered

How a 660-tonne steel pendulum keeps Taipei 101 steady in super typhoons 🏢

#engineering #structuralengineering #architecture #physics #howitsengineered

Read replicas explained: when your database can't keep up with reads, copy it. Writes go to the primary, reads spread across replicas, and replication lag is why a new comment can look missing for a second.
Does your app read more than it writes? 📚

#readreplicas #database #postgresql #systemdesign #scaling

N+1 queries explained: your page makes 101 database trips when 2 would do, one query for the list plus one per order. Fetch the related rows together in one query, or turn on eager loading in your ORM.
How many queries does your slowest page run? 🔍

#nplusone #sql #database #systemdesign #backend

Connection pooling explained: why your app shows errors at peak traffic when the database is fine. Open a few database connections, keep them open and reuse them, and keep the total under Postgres' connection limit.
Does your app use a connection pool? 🚕

#connectionpooling #postgresql #database #systemdesign #backend

How noise-cancelling headphones work: tiny microphones hear the engine, a chip flips that sound wave upside down, and the speaker plays the opposite. At your ear the two waves meet and much of the roar cancels out. In 1978, Amar Bose sketched the maths on a flight to Boston because the engines drowned out his music.
The quiet you hear is two sound waves cancelling each other. 🎧

#noisecancelling #headphones #bose #howitworks #systemdesign

How tap to pay works: your card has no battery. The card machine makes a magnetic field, and a coil hidden around the edge of your card turns it into just enough electricity to wake the chip. The chip answers with your card number plus a one-time code that only works for this payment.
On the London Tube, the gate checks the card on the spot and the bank checks the payment later. 🚇

#contactless #tapandpay #nfc #howitworks #systemdesign

How a capacitive touchscreen works: a hidden grid under the glass feels your finger change a tiny electric signal, so gloves fail and a snack sausage can fool it. Has your wet screen ever tapped by itself?

#capacitivetouch #phonescreen #howthingswork #scienceexplained #everydaytech

How GPS finds you: your phone never talks to the satellites. About 30 of them keep broadcasting where they are and exactly when each signal left. Your phone times each signal, turns that into distance, and finds the one spot where the spheres overlap. Until 2000, the US made public GPS wrong on purpose, by about a street.
The satellites say where they are. Your phone works out where you are. 🛰️

#gps #satellites #navigation #howitworks #systemdesign

How Google Maps knows about traffic: no cameras. Phones navigating with Maps share where they are and how fast they're moving. When lots of them slow down on one road, that stretch turns red. In 2020, artist Simon Weckert walked 99 phones down an empty Berlin street in a wagon, and Maps showed a jam.
Next time you're stuck in traffic, you might be one of the dots. 🚗

#googlemaps #traffic #navigation #howitworks #systemdesign

Query optimization explained: SELECT * pulls a million rows to show 10 orders. Ask the database only for the rows and columns your page needs, then check the query plan with EXPLAIN.
Is your app fetching data it throws away? ⚡

#queryoptimization #sql #database #systemdesign #backend

The airline said her bag was safe. Her AirTag said otherwise. How AirTag works: no GPS, no SIM. It pings over Bluetooth, and any nearby iPhone, even yours, sends its location to Apple, encrypted so only the owner can read it.
Flying soon? Would you put one in your checked bag? ✈️

#airtag #findmy #lostluggage #howitworks #systemdesign

How Shazam knows the song: it turns sound into a map of pitch over time, keeps only the brightest points (like stars), and links pairs of stars into tiny codes. Those codes are the recording's fingerprint, matched against millions of songs. In 2002 there was no app: you dialled 2580 and got the song name by text.
That's why humming it won't work. 🎵

#shazam #music #audiofingerprint #howitworks #systemdesign

Database indexing explained: one line of SQL, CREATE INDEX, turns a full table scan of 100 million rows into a 3-hop lookup, but every extra index slows down your writes.
Which column does your app search by the most? 🔍

#databaseindexing #sql #postgresql #systemdesign #backend

The weather server stopped answering for one second. Then thousands of apps tried again at the same moment, and it went down for real.

Retrying means trying again. It helps when a connection drops for a moment. But thousands of apps trying again instantly, over and over, can overwhelm the server. That's a retry storm.

Fix one: stop when it works, or after three retries.
Fix two: wait longer each time. One second, then two, then four, so the server can recover.
Fix three: add a little randomness to each wait, so the apps don't all come back together.

Does your app retry forever when a request fails? Tell me below 🌩️

#retries #backend #coding #programming #systemdesign

You changed one letter in your code. Two minutes later, your whole app was down.

The change went straight to your users, with nothing in between to catch the mistake.

CI/CD automates the steps between changing your code and releasing it. First it builds your app. That fails? It stops. Then automated tests check things like whether login still works. A check fails? It stops. Everything passes? The update is ready to release, automatically or after someone approves it.

So that typo? If the build or a test catches it, your users never see it.

What's the smallest change that ever broke your app? Tell me below ⚙️

#cicd #devops #coding #programming #systemdesign

You texted a friend whose phone is dead. One grey tick. So where is that message right now?

It's waiting in a queue: a line on a server where messages sit until someone picks them up. You drop the message in and move on. The receiver doesn't need to be online.

When your friend's phone comes back, it picks the messages up and confirms each one arrived. Only then is it removed from the queue.

Shops queue work too. Checkout drops each order in a queue, and background workers handle them at their own pace, so a rush waits in line instead of piling onto the server.

Like a post office holding your letters until you come to collect them.

Where would a queue save your app during a rush? Tell me below 📬

#messagequeue #backend #coding #programming #systemdesign

Your app takes two seconds to load its data. But the second time you open the page, it's almost instant. What changed?

The first time, the server gets the answer from the database and waits. Then it saves a copy in a faster store: a cache. Next time, it checks the cache first. Copy found? That's a cache hit, and there's no trip to the database.

Like a sticky note on your desk, instead of walking to the filing room every time.

The catch: a copied price can go out of date. So developers set copies to expire, or clear them when the price changes.

What's the slowest page in your app? Tell me below ⚡

#caching #backend #coding #programming #systemdesign

You asked an AI chatbot a question, and the answer appeared word by word, like someone typing live. How does the server keep sending?

If the server waited to send the whole answer at once, you'd stare at a blank screen for seconds.

With server-sent events, your app asks once and the server keeps that reply open. Every time it has a few new words, it sends them right away in a small message called an event, and your app adds them to the screen. It only flows one way, from the server to you. To send something back, your app makes a new request.

Like a news ticker: you tune in once, and the headlines keep rolling in.

What would you stream live in your app? Tell me below ⚡

#serversentevents #webdev #coding #programming #systemdesign

Your app asked the server for new messages, and the server didn't answer for thirty seconds. On purpose. Why?

Without it, your app keeps asking, and most answers are "nothing new". That's a lot of wasted trips.

Long polling flips that. The server holds your question and waits. The moment a message arrives, it answers, and your app asks again right away. If nothing happens before a time limit (say 30 seconds), it answers "nothing yet" and your app asks again.

Like a kid asking "are we there yet?" every minute, versus asking once and getting the answer the moment you arrive.

Have you ever built a bot that polls for updates? Tell me below 🤖

#longpolling #webdev #coding #programming #systemdesign

Your friend hit send, and it popped up on your phone instantly. You never refreshed. So how did your app know?

Normally your app asks the server a question and gets one answer. Want something new? Ask again. The server can't speak first.

A WebSocket keeps one connection open, like a phone call nobody hangs up. Either side can talk any time, so the server pushes your friend's message to you the moment it arrives.

The catch: every open connection uses server memory, and when your signal drops, your app has to reconnect.

What would you build with a live connection? Tell me below 💬

#websockets #webdev #coding #programming #systemdesign

3 AM. Nobody's awake, and your app just emailed 10,000 people their receipts. Who pressed the button?

Nobody. A cron job did. It's a scheduled task, like a repeating alarm for your server. You set the timing once (0 3 * * * means every day at 3 AM), and when it rings, the server runs your code.

One catch: put the same schedule on two servers and both alarms ring. Everyone gets two receipts. Keep the schedule in one place. Linux has cron built in, and Kubernetes has CronJobs.

What does your app do at 3 AM? Tell me below ⏰

#cronjob #linux #coding #programming #systemdesign

You tapped Pay twice on bad Wi-Fi. So why weren't you charged twice?

Your app gives each payment a unique number and sends that same number on every retry. The server saves the number with the result. When it sees the number again, it sends back the saved answer instead of charging again. That's idempotency: doing it twice has the same effect as doing it once. Stripe supports this with an Idempotency-Key.

Like pressing an elevator button that's already lit.

Ever been charged twice for something? Tell me below 💳

#idempotency #coding #programming #systemdesign #backend

Your app has 10 servers, and bots can't find a single one. All they ever reach is one machine: a reverse proxy.

Every request hits the proxy first. Your servers stay private with no public address, popular pages come straight from its cache, and it routes /api and /images to different servers. NGINX and Cloudflare do this for millions of sites.

A forward proxy hides your IP from the website. A reverse proxy hides the servers from you.

Did you know your requests never touch the real servers? Tell me below 🛡️

#reverseproxy #nginx #coding #programming #systemdesign

Your flight and hotel are paid for. Then the car booking fails. Who gets your money back?

Each booking is a separate program with its own records, so there is no shared undo. The saga pattern runs the steps one by one, and every step has a cleanup. When the car fails, it cleans up backwards: cancel the hotel, cancel the flight, request the refunds. Those cleanups are called compensating actions, and you write them. AWS Step Functions can run the whole saga.

Like a travel agent who cancels your trip in reverse ✈️

#sagapattern #microservices #systemdesign #distributedsystems #backend

What is a dead letter queue? The simple version, in 40 seconds.

One broken order fails every time, your app keeps retrying it, and every order behind it piles up. That's a poison message. A dead letter queue fixes it: you set a limit, and after that many failures the message is moved aside so the rest keep flowing. Later you fix the cause and send it back. Amazon SQS and RabbitMQ both support it.

The post office bin for undeliverable mail 📮

#deadletterqueue #messagequeue #systemdesign #backend #aws

How does load balancing work? How apps survive going viral, in 35 seconds.

You run 10 copies of your app, and a load balancer decides which one gets each request. Round robin takes turns. Least connections picks the server with the fewest open connections. Health checks skip a server that stops answering, and you can add servers without changing the address users visit.

The supermarket manager of your backend 🛒

#loadbalancing #systemdesign #devops #backend #scalability

Rate limiting, the simple version: why your app should say "too many requests".

A bot hits your login page 50,000 times a minute guessing passwords. A rate limiter counts each user's tries and, past the limit, answers with 429 Too Many Requests until the time window resets. Real users keep getting in. GitHub, OpenAI and Stripe all do it.

Like a bouncer with a clicker 🚪

#ratelimiting #apisecurity #systemdesign #backend #webdevelopment

One update blue-screened 8.5 million computers. All at the same time 💥

Airports, banks, hospitals. Down.

Coal miners had a fix: send a canary down first 🐤 If the bird stops singing, everyone gets out.

A canary release does the same for code:
🐤 Ship the new version to 1% first
👀 Watch for crashes, errors, reboots
↩️ Something spikes? Roll back automatically
📈 All good? 5%, then 25%, then everyone

That's Argo Rollouts and AWS CodeDeploy.

Does your team ship to everyone at once? 👇

#systemdesign #softwareengineering #devops #crowdstrike #canaryrelease

You tap Place Order. One second later your email, tracking page and reward points all update. But nobody told them to 🛒

The slow way: every service keeps asking the order service, “anything new?” All day. Almost every answer is no, so thousands of wasted calls drown it. Calling them directly instead? Then the order service has to know everyone.

Event-driven architecture fixes it:
📢 The order service just announces a fact: “Order placed.” That’s an event
📜 A log keeps every event, in order
⚡ Email, tracking and rewards each react on their own

🔔 Like a doorbell: you don’t keep checking the door. It rings, you answer.

⏪ A service was down? It reads the log and catches up
🆕 A new service? It replays past events
🙈 And the order service never changes. It doesn’t even know who’s listening

That’s Apache Kafka and Amazon EventBridge.

Which of your services is still asking “anything new?” Comment below 👇

#systemdesign #softwareengineering #backend #eventdriven #kafka

One post. Two million followers. One message. 📮

Your post service shouldn’t be notifying followers, sending emails and updating feeds itself. Do it all in a row, and one slow email keeps your post button spinning.

“Just use a message queue?” Nope. A queue hands each message to ONE worker. You need every feature to hear it.

That’s Pub/Sub:
📣 Publish once to a topic. The post service is done instantly
📬 Every subscriber gets its own copy, all at the same time
🧩 Add a feature by subscribing it. Zero changes to the publisher

📻 Think radio station: one broadcast, every tuned-in radio hears it.

You’ll find it as Google Cloud Pub/Sub and Amazon SNS.

Queue or Pub/Sub: which one does your app actually need? Tell me below 👇

#systemdesign #softwareengineering #backend #pubsub #coding

Your app asked a server for the weather, and nothing came back. How long should it wait? ⏳

By default, it might wait forever. Python’s requests won’t time out unless you pass a timeout, and Go’s default http client is the same.

Waiting isn’t free:
🧵 The slow call holds a thread while the spinner spins
📥 Every request stuck behind it holds another
🔴 Run out of threads and your app stops answering everyone

⏱️ A timeout is a deadline: the longest you’ll wait before calling it a failure. timeout=3 means after 3 seconds you stop waiting.
✅ Then handle it: show a clear error, or fall back to the forecast you saved earlier.

Have you ever had a request hang forever with no error? Comment below 👇

#coding #programming #softwareengineer #systemdesign #backend

One slow service took down the whole app. Not broken. Just slow. ⚡

Every request waits on it, each one holds a thread, threads run out, and the server stops answering everyone. That’s a cascading failure. Retries make it worse.

The fix is a circuit breaker, borrowed from your house:
🟢 Closed: calls go through and failures get counted
🔴 Open: too many failures, so calls fail instantly and the page hides that part
🟡 Half-open: after a cooldown, a few test calls decide whether it closes again

Netflix built Hystrix for this. Today Resilience4j does it in a few lines.

Have you ever had one slow service take down your whole app? Comment below 👇

#coding #programming #softwareengineer #systemdesign #microservices

Your app froze at 3 AM. Still running, not answering anyone. And something restarted it before anyone woke up. 🥶

The trap: running isn’t the same as working. A frozen app still looks alive, nothing crashed, so nothing restarts it.

The fix: keep asking it “are you okay?” Like a nurse checking your pulse. That’s a health check.

💓 Alive? Every few seconds it calls your app’s health page. Three misses in a row? Restart
🚦 Ready? A copy that’s still starting up says “not yet”, and traffic skips it until it is

In Kubernetes these are liveness and readiness probes: a few lines in your config.

#coding #programming #softwareengineer #systemdesign #kubernetes

Your service restarted. Same code, new address. And every call to it failed. 💥

The bug: the address was written into the code. In the cloud, servers restart and move all the time, so that address goes stale.

The fix: save the name, not the number. Like your phone contacts. That’s service discovery.

📝 Register: when a service starts, it tells a registry “I’m payments, here’s my address”
🔍 Look up: before every call, the caller asks the registry where payments is right now
💓 Check: the registry keeps pinging every copy. One stops answering? It’s off the list

In Kubernetes it’s built in: call payments by name and it routes you to the right address.

Your app crashed at 3 AM. By the time you woke up, it was already back. Nobody touched it. 😴

With Docker alone, a crashed container stays dead until you restart it by hand. Kubernetes is the robot that does it for you: you say what you want, it keeps it that way. Like a thermostat.

🩹 Heal: one copy crashes, a new one starts in seconds
📈 Scale: traffic spikes, it adds copies. Traffic drops, it removes them
🔄 Update: new version rolls out one copy at a time, zero downtime

Docker packs the box. Kubernetes runs the fleet.
Built by Google, offered by every big cloud (AWS, Google Cloud, Azure).

One service in your food app forgot to check the login. Now anyone can see everyone’s orders. 💥

Your app isn’t one program. It’s small services: users, menu, payments, delivery. If your phone calls each one directly, every service has to check your login on its own. Miss one, and the door’s wide open.

The fix? One front door. An API gateway. Like airport check-in: nobody boards without passing it.
🪪 Check ID: it checks your login once, then passes your ID along
🚦 Count: one user spams refresh? Blocked. Everyone else stays fast
🔀 Route: one tap on Order goes to 4 services, and it stitches the answers together

A gateway is a reverse proxy that understands your API.
Kong and Amazon API Gateway run it for real companies.

Have you ever shipped an endpoint with no auth check? Be honest 👇

#coding #programming #softwareengineer #webdevelopment #backend

It works on your laptop. You put it on a server and it crashes. Same code. 💥

The code isn’t the problem. Everything around it is: a different Node version, a library you installed months ago and forgot, a missing .env file.

The fix? Don’t send just the code. Send the whole machine. That’s Docker:
📝 Recipe: a Dockerfile lists exactly which Node, which libraries and which files your app needs
❄️ Build: Docker freezes all of it into an image, a snapshot of everything your app needs
🚀 Run: that image runs anywhere as a container. Laptop, server, your teammate’s PC. Identical.

The image is the box. The container is the box, running.
